items.title: Kent Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] I was talking to Clyde Kerr just now about the family tradition in New Orleans.

ctx.x: Right. A violin and a fiddle player. You know most violinists call themselves fiddle players, so yeah that’s an interesting dichotomy there.

I was talking to Clyde Kerr just now about the family tradition in New Orleans. It’s unbelievable to me, the number of families. It’s almost like a family that would always have carpenters or bricklayers or some families have musicians.

That’s an interesting analogy. I’ve never really thought of it that way. You know I guess in certain areas of the country where certain livelihoods or occupations would dominate, and obviously in New Orleans the music has always been a dominant influence in terms of our culture. And I think that’s one of the reasons why families have evolved so, because outside of my family, the Jordan family, were my mom grew up in a family of 16 kids, if you can believe that, but everybody played an instrument or sang.
